title: Batching & KV prefetch scenario workshop - Edenfield Ventures scoping
summary: Intro scoping call to map Edenfield's ecomm search assistant workload to Redwood Optimize recommendations. Focused on batching strategies, prefix/KV cache sizing, hit-rate assumptions, and a cost-simulation they'd like us to run against their query distribution. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share sandbox cost spreadsheet, run two simulation scenarios (high-concurrency web, multi-turn chat sessions), and schedule a 45m pilot kickoff next week to run in their dev VPC or Redwood Dedicated trial.
topics: batch size vs tail latency tradeoffs

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-08-03
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Samantha (Redwood), Devon (Redwood SE), Maya (Edenfield), Liam (Edenfield), Priya (Edenfield CTO)

Auto-summary (may be partial): We walked through a couple of cost sims, discussed KV hit-rate assumptions, and captured action items for a pilot.

[00:00] Samantha Ortiz: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Sam from Redwood, I'll hand off to Devon for the technical runthrough but first quick intros
[00:22] Maya Chen: Hi this is Maya, Head of ML at Edenfield, thanks for doing this. We're mainly trying to figure out how to get the search assistant to scale without blowing our inferencing budget.
[00:35] Liam O'Connor: Liam here, platform eng. Our traffic is spiky, most of the day is low qps but we get bursts at campaign times. Latency SLO is 150ms p95 for the search completions.
[00:48] Devon Park: Great, thanks. Today we'll go over batching strategies and prefix / KV prefetch so you can see the tradeoffs in cost and tail latency. I'll call out what we usually change in Optimize and in the console.
[01:10] Priya Rao: Quick question on the SLO, 150ms p95 — is that for single-shot completions? or multi-turn sessions too?
[01:18] Maya Chen: Mostly single-shot for search ranking, but some flows are multi-turn clarification, yes.
[01:26] Devon Park: Okay makes sense, we'll sketch both. First, can you confirm typical prompt lengths and distribution?
[01:36] Maya Chen: We'll email a histogram, but avg prompt tokens ~60, responses around 40, and hit-rate on user intent heuristics about 30% where you can short-circuit before model call.
[01:51] Devon Park: Good context. So the two levers we tend to tune: batching (how many requests we accumulate in the runtime before executing a batch) and prefix/KV caching (store KV from common prefixes to avoid redoing attention for warm states).
[02:10] Samantha Ortiz: I'll drop a link to the cost spreadsheet after this call — it's the one Devon will use to run the sims.
[02:18] Liam O'Connor: Cool. Can you just briefly describe continuous batching vs fixed-window batching?
[02:26] Devon Park: Sure — continuous batching (aka dynamic) aggregates requests as they arrive up to a target batch size or latency cap; fixed-window batches requests within a time window. Continuous tends to give better throughput with variable arrival rates, fixed-window can be simpler and slightly better for tail-latency if you pick a tight window but loses throughput. For your spiky traffic we'd recommend continuous with a soft latency cap of 40ms to meet your 150ms p95 end-to-end.
[02:58] Maya Chen: Wait, 40ms cap for the runtime alone? That leaves how much for network and app?
[03:05] Devon Park: Right so runtime budget maybe 30-60ms depending on model; we usually reserve ~100ms for the rest of the pipeline to meet 150ms p95. We'll show the math in the sim.
[03:18] Samantha Ortiz: Quick aside — are you planning to run on Dedicated GPUs or hosted?
[03:23] Priya Rao: We were thinking Dedicated for predictability, but can consider hosted for the pilot to get rolling faster. Cost and isolation are both important.
[03:34] Devon Park: Great, Dedicated makes sense for predictable throughput; for the pilot hosted is often faster to spin up and we can mirror the matching SKU in Dedicated later. The cost sim will show both.
[03:48] [04:00] Devon Park: Now prefix/KV caching — we typically look at sessionization: how many requests per session, what percent of sessions share prefixes long enough to justify prefetch. For search assistants, caching the first 16-32 tokens of the prompt or a canonicalized query representation often yields high hit rates.
[04:23] Maya Chen: Our search queries have a lot of canonicalization (product IDs, filters) so there may be a decent hit rate; but how do you size the KV cache?
[04:33] Devon Park: Two axes: capacity and eviction policy. You size capacity by looking at working set (unique prefixes in high-frequency windows) and tune TTL/eviction. In the sim we'll estimate required GPU RAM for KV entries and the expected hit-rate. We usually present a curve: hit-rate vs memory vs cost.
[04:54] Liam O'Connor: Can you show an example number? like with a 64GB KV pool what hit-rate do you expect?
[05:02] Devon Park: Rough rule: if your top 5-10% of prefixes make up 50-60% of traffic, a 64GB KV pool for a modern 7B style model could yield 30-45% hit rates for typical ecomm queries. But it's very data dependent — that's why we asked for the histogram.
[05:25] Maya Chen: And what about multi-turn chat? If the user keeps clarifying, does KV help?
[05:31] Devon Park: Yes, session affinity + KV helps a lot for multi-turn. If the session stays on the same context, KV hits are much higher because the prefix context is mostly unchanged. Also prefetching KV at session start when you know likely flows can amortize the cost.
[05:50] Samantha Ortiz: Quick interruption — there's an assumption here about model size. Which model families are you comfortable testing?
[05:57] Priya Rao: We'd like to test a small-ish high-quality model and one quantized variant. Maybe redwood-ensemble-1 (baseline) and open-quant-7B as a cheaper baseline.
[06:10] Devon Park: Perfect, we'll include both. In the sim we'll show tokens/sec per GPU, expected throughput, and cost per million tokens for each.
[06:21] [06:40] Devon Park: Now cost model basics — inputs are: request volume distribution, avg prompt/response tokens, desired latency SLO, KV hit-rate assumptions, batch target size, and model SKU/quantization. From that we run an admission simulation that outputs expected GPU hours, avg latency, and cost.
[06:55] Maya Chen: For admission sim, do you simulate real arrival patterns? or a Poisson assumption?
[07:02] Devon Park: We can do both. For initial sims we support Poisson or empirical distributions if you provide request timestamps/histogram — which gives much better results for spikes.
[07:15] Liam O'Connor: We'll provide the histogram. Also curious how prefetch costs are accounted — prefetching sounds like extra tokens to generate KV?
[07:26] Devon Park: Yes prefetch has an upfront cost: you might generate KV for a predicted next prompt, or precompute a reused prefix. We model prefetch cost as an additional token cost per session; the sim balances prefetch overhead vs hit-rate savings.
[07:42] Priya Rao: Any examples where prefetch backfired?
[07:45] Devon Park: If your prefix space is huge and predictions are low quality you pay prefetch cost without hit-rate gains; we usually throttle prefetch to heavy-hitter prefixes or use a confidence threshold from downstream heuristics.
[07:58] [08:10] Maya Chen: Ok that makes sense. For our case we suspect ~40% canonical prefixes and maybe a 15-20% prefetch false positive rate.
[08:20] Devon Park: Good input. We'll run a worst/best case scenario. Now let's run through a short walkthrough — I'm going to narrate two scenarios: 1) web search workload: short single-shot completions, high concurrency spikes; 2) chat assistant: multi-turn longer context, session affinity.
[08:38] Devon Park: Scenario 1: web search. Assumptions: avg prompt 60 tokens, response 30 tokens, 400 qps peak during spikes, 40 qps baseline. Target p95 150ms end-to-end. Batching: continuous with target batch size 8 and latency cap 35ms. KV prefetch: disabled initially, then simulate with a 30% hit-rate candidate with prefetch cost of 12 tokens/session.
[09:08] Devon Park: Result: without KV prefetch you need more GPU instances to keep tail latency down. With KV prefetch and a 30% hit-rate, throughput per GPU increases ~1.6x and modeled cost drops ~28% in Dedicated pricing. These are illustrative numbers.
[09:28] Samantha Ortiz: Note — numbers will change by model selection and quantization. We'll include alt columns.
[09:35] [09:45] Maya Chen: Scenario 2?
[09:46] Devon Park: Scenario 2: chat. Assumptions: avg prompt 120 tokens, response 80 tokens, session length avg 4 turns, session affinity 85% across turns. Batching: batch target 4 due to interactive needs, latency cap 50ms, KV cache sized to hold ~20k entries.
[10:10] Devon Park: Result: KV cache yields very high hit-rate across turns — often 60-70% depending on canonicalization — and reduces per-turn token compute significantly. Cost drop in that scenario could be 35-50% versus no-cache. But with small batch targets throughput is lower, so Dedicated sizing needs to reflect concurrent sessions instead of pure qps.
[10:34] Liam O'Connor: That last line is important — we care about concurrency more than raw qps for chat.
[10:39] Devon Park: Exactly. We'll highlight concurrency provisioning in the sim.
[10:43] [11:00] Maya Chen: Any impacts on model quality from caching or quantization?
[11:05] Devon Park: For caching there is no quality loss — it's just reusing computed KV. Quantization can slightly affect generation quality, depends on model and quant recipe. We recommend running evals on your prompt set for any quantized candidate. Redwood Optimize includes a quality-monitoring check so you can tie regression alerts to prompt sets.
[11:28] Priya Rao: Security and data residency — if we store KV in your hosted service, how is it protected?
[11:35] Samantha Ortiz: Good question. For Hosted we encrypt at rest and in transit, access controls, and SOC2 compliance. For Dedicated or Private we can run KV on customer-owned VPC and integrate with your KMS/HSM — that keeps data in your control. We'll include our security brief in the follow-up.
[11:55] Devon Park: Also note that we support per-tenant isolation in Dedicated so KV doesn't cross customers.
[12:02] [12:20] Maya Chen: Great. Can you also explain autoscaling behavior when KV prefetch increases memory needs?
[12:28] Devon Park: Sure — in Dedicated you can configure autoscale to add nodes when memory pressure or latency crosses thresholds. We recommend alerting on KV eviction rates and miss surge. For the pilot, we'll target conservative memory configs then tune.
[12:44] [13:00] Priya Rao: Do you have guidance for initial KV capacity for our dataset size?
[13:06] Devon Park: We'll estimate from your unique prefix counts in the histogram. As a starting heuristic: allocate KV memory to cover the top 3-5% of prefixes that represent 40-50% of calls. We'll run the numbers in the spreadsheet.
[13:21] [13:30] Liam O'Connor: One more — what's the rollout strategy if caching causes unforeseen regressions? Can you SRE/fallback to non-cached mode?
[13:39] Devon Park: Yes we support canarying and automatic fallbacks. In the Console you can configure rollouts by routing policy: start a small percent on cached variant, monitor quality/latency, and auto rollback if regressions exceed thresholds.
[13:56] [14:10] Samantha Ortiz: I'll capture that in the next steps.
[14:16] Devon Park: Ok quick demo notes — console has a simulation tab in Optimize where you upload or paste a distribution and toggle KV settings. It will produce a CSV of GPU-hours and cost under Hosted/Dedicated pricing.
[14:34] Maya Chen: Any gotchas on the CSV format?
[14:38] Devon Park: We accept a histogram (time bucket, qps) or raw timestamps. CSV template we'll send.
[14:47] [15:00] Maya Chen: Regarding pilot, we want to run in our dev VPC to validate network latency — is that supported?
[15:07] Samantha Ortiz: Yes — for Private/Dedicated we can run in your VPC; for Hosted pilot we can run a regional dedicated pool that peeks into your VPC via private link if needed. We'll coordinate with your infra.
[15:24] [15:45] Devon Park: Now, some practical numbers I'll call out that we'll include in the follow-up sim: tokens/sec for redwood-ensemble-1 at sequence length 256 on an A100-ish SKU ~ 1,800-2,400 tokens/sec depending on quantization, 7B quantized ~3,000-4,500 tokens/sec. Batch shapes and KV-hit assumptions change those by +/-30%.
[16:10] Maya Chen: Nice. If we do the pilot on Dedicated, what's the minimum commitment?
[16:16] Samantha Ortiz: For Dedicated it's flexible but we usually recommend a minimum 1 or 2-node reserved baseline for enterprise; pricing discussion will be in the commercial follow-up. For pilot we can enable a trial pool to validate the sim.
[16:30] [16:50] Liam O'Connor: Ok, let's talk timeline — if we send histogram by Thursday, when can we expect the sims?
[16:57] Devon Park: We'll start sims when we get histograms — initial slides and CSV by EOD Friday if we get it Thursday. A more thorough run Monday-Wednesday next week for the two scenarios.
[17:10] Maya Chen: Works.
[17:16] [17:40] Priya Rao: A couple of governance questions — audit logs for who can prefetch or change KV settings?
[17:48] Samantha Ortiz: Console has RBAC and audit trails; any change to Optimize configs is logged with actor and timestamp. We can demo audit logs in the follow-up.
[17:59] Devon Park: Also we have an eval-run feature that ties quality regressions to a specific rollout so you can trace which change impacted outputs.
[18:12] [18:30] Maya Chen: Good. Anything else for the simulation assumptions?
[18:34] Devon Park: Please include: raw timestamps or histogram, avg prompt/response tokens, sessionization indicator, model preference list, and if you have any heavy-hitter query list (top 100 canonical prefixes) that would help.
[18:48] Maya Chen: We'll compile and send later today.
[18:53] [19:10] Samantha Ortiz: Recap — Redwood to run two sims (web search + chat), share spreadsheet, include Hosted vs Dedicated columns, include KV capacity memory estimate and hit-rate curves, security brief, and schedule pilot kickoff.
[19:27] Maya Chen: Sounds good. Thank you.
[19:32] Priya Rao: Appreciate it.
[19:36] Devon Park: Last quick note — if you want we can also run a micro-benchmark on a 1-hour sample in our sandbox to validate token/sec numbers; it's useful if you have concerns about model perf variance.
[19:51] Liam O'Connor: Yes please add that as an option.
[19:55] [20:10] Samantha Ortiz: I'll include that in action items. We'll also attach a sample console link for the team.
[20:18] Devon Park: Great. Any final quick questions?
[20:21] Maya Chen: None from me.
[20:23] Priya Rao: No.
[20:25] Samantha Ortiz: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up by email with the spreadsheet and a proposed pilot slot. Bye.

End of transcript.
questions: How do you size KV cache given a long tail of prefixes?
